title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Medical equipment cleaning (external only)
audience: Solo operators and team owners who want more external equipment cleaning work from clinics and care settings that fit their service, area and batch size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, setting type, batch size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a need for external equipment cleaning is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what equipment work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want more of. Write down the settings you can serve, such as clinics and care settings that authorise external cleaning of their equipment, the batch sizes you can handle, the postcodes you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each setting needs a batch. Write down what you will not take: reprocessing or disinfection of reusable devices, invasive devices, and any decision to release equipment for patient use sit outside this course. A regular batch on a route you already run is worth far more than a single large job across town. If you cannot state these criteria, you cannot tell a good lead from a poor one.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit against the written criteria: is it inside your service area, does it have a repeat need, can you reach the person who makes the buying decision, such as a practice manager or facility manager, and does the work fall inside your licence and insurance. Record the date each entry was added and where its contact details came from. Use only contact details published for business use. Business.gov.au suggests one short profile for each segment (24 September 2024). Before you contact anyone, confirm the scope, your capacity and the deadline, as Business Queensland advises before sending a quote (16 November 2022). Do not buy or harvest contact lists. ACMA's Spam Act guidance says buying a list does not remove the duty to show consent (last updated 28 March 2019, an older source). The research found no equipment-cleaning prospect directory.

instruction.heading: Watch for public signals that a need is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need for external equipment cleaning more likely soon. Examples include a planning application for alterations to a clinic or care home on a route you already run, a new clinic opening on a street where you already work, a change of occupier at a site you already service, or a published tender for facility services. Use signals to choose when to make contact, not to build a profile of any individual or member of staff. Council planning permit registers can show applications at application stage. The City of Casey register on Victoria's open-data portal is one example, and each council publishes its own (DataVic, metadata 15 November 2023, last updated 5 November 2026). Building permit activity data can be filtered by suburb and used for area-level targeting, not individual contact (Data Vic, last updated 28 August 2026). In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and offers alerts (last updated 7 August 2026), and AusTender does the same federally. The research found no tender source for equipment cleaning, so whether clinics or care settings buy through these portals is unconfirmed.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message does three things. It states how you came to know about the facility or the notice. It makes one specific observation you can verify from public view or from the facility's own published material, such as a notice about works or a listing with an obvious gap in its service range. It then offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined list of items or a short call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and never refer to a named patient, resident or staff member. Where the message goes by email or text, check the consent and unsubscribe rules first. The ACCC's 2026 review found that about 80 per cent of respondents said unsolicited selling seldom gave useful information or offers, and that about 71 per cent of salespeople identified themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026). An honest, identified approach is therefore a practical advantage as well as a compliance step.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be. The research gives no source for a particular interval, so set one, record it and review whether it works. Stopping is part of the approach. If a contact says no, or asks you to stop, remove it from the list at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid work, and move your effort toward them. Silence is not consent to keep contacting someone.

procedure: Write the setting, area, batch size and repeat-need criteria for the equipment work you want, and list the work you will not take.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules, the Do Not Call rules for calls and the licence rules before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on your fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A small business covers three suburbs. A council planning application for alterations to a medical centre appears on the register, and the centre's published business email address is on its website. The register entry does not show clearly what the alterations involve.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner send a sales message now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner does not send a sales email just because the address is published. ACMA's guidance says publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages, so the owner first checks whether the centre has agreed to receive them or has invited contact. If neither applies, the owner waits for an invitation or uses a route the centre has agreed to. Phone calls to registered numbers are limited by the Do Not Call Register rules, so the owner washes any call list against the register and calls only in permitted hours: weekdays 9 am to 8 pm and Saturdays 9 am to 5 pm, with no calls on Sundays or public holidays (2018 DNCR guide). The owner confirms what the alterations involve before saying anything about them, does not enter the site and does not contact staff using private details. Any message that does go out names the application, says how the business learned of it, offers one batch of external cleaning for the centre's listed equipment, and asks one question. It does not offer reprocessing or any decision about releasing equipment.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for setting type, service area, batch size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety and infection-control rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual, such as a staff member or patient, to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service that you are not licensed or insured to deliver, such as reprocessing.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance before outreach, and remove any service that falls outside your cover from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. Do not offer reprocessing, disinfection of reusable devices or clinical decisions in outreach. This lesson does not grant any licence. Licence rules differ between states and territories, so check the rule for each one you work in.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA says marketing messages need consent, the consent should be recorded, every message must identify the sender and include correct contact details, and unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days (ACMA, read 2026-11-03). The Act text was not read for this research, so check it before sending.

Public listings and public notices do not by themselves permit contact. The OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7) says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules where the Privacy Act applies (page modified 16 October 2023; version 1.1 dated 22 July 2019). Whether the Act applies to a small business is unconfirmed in the research. Use only published business contact details, and stop when someone objects.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the equipment work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A clinic group with several sites inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public notice shows planned works at a clinic in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the clinic's manager about the works, by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each staff member using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for the works
Go into the clinic to look at the work before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a clinic, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending
